tldr: This paper establishes a unified discrete Riemannian framework on polyhedral surface meshes (polygons) from CAD or 3D reconstruction—handling edge and vertex singularities without breaking—and applies it to dynamic movement primitives (DMPs), Gaussian processes (GPs), and Riemannian flow matching (RFM) to achieve high-accuracy motion generation and real-robot transfer.
hero_caption: A 2D trajectory hand-drawn on a tablet is transferred geometrically and seamlessly onto various 3D-printed surface meshes with different curvatures and undulations, and drawn using a Franka Research 3 manipulator. Skills demonstrated on a flat plane adapt accurately onto discrete surfaces with bumps and sharp, non-differentiable creases.
overview:
When robots perform tasks like wiping, polishing, or drawing, their motions unfold across the surfaces of objects or the environment. However, conventional learning from demonstration (LfD) and motion planning often learn trajectories in flat Euclidean space. They then force the motion onto the surface using post-hoc projection or impedance control. This approach struggles when the surface geometry changes. Geometric learning on smooth Riemannian manifolds has been proposed, but real-world shapes from CAD models or RGB-D cameras are polyhedral meshes (discrete surfaces) where derivatives cannot be defined at vertices and edges.

Drawing on discrete differential geometry, the authors construct a unified discrete Riemannian operational framework that remains well-defined across faces, edges, and vertices of meshes. They rigorously define tangent cones extending local tangent spaces, exponential maps based on straightest geodesics, and parallel transport along geodesics. Furthermore, they extend this framework to three major robotics learning paradigms: Dynamic Movement Primitives (DMPs), Gaussian Processes (GPs), and Riemannian Flow Matching (RFM).

In simulation, the method eliminates rotational drift found in prior mesh-based DMPs and overcomes the smoothness assumptions and vertex-only restrictions of conventional Laplace-Beltrami operator-based kernels. Real-robot experiments confirm successful transfer: user-drawn characters on a tablet are drawn across diverse surfaces, and unknown surfaces reconstructed online via an RGB-D camera are autonomously polished with a sponge.
contributions: Proposed a geometrically consistent discrete Riemannian operator framework (logarithmic map, exponential map, parallel transport, and tangent cone projection) that rigorously handles singularities at polyhedral mesh faces, edges, and vertices.

Constructed a discrete surface DMP that encodes the forcing term within a fixed tangent cone and reconstructs it via parallel transport, eliminating limit-cycle drift and instability on curved surfaces seen in prior methods.

Established a geodesic distance-based Gaussian process (GP) and its practical admissibility control, enabling regression evaluation at arbitrary mesh locations—including face interiors—without relying on Laplace-Beltrami operator eigenfunction expansions.
Formulated Riemannian Flow Matching (RFM) on discrete surfaces using geodesic premetrics, halving training time compared to spectral baselines while improving generative sample quality.

sections.heading: Why Should Robots Learn Directly on Discrete Polyhedral Surfaces?
sections.summary: Contact tasks like wiping and polishing depend heavily on surface geometry, yet prior methods often treat surfaces merely as external constraints. Because real-world 3D meshes are non-smooth and contain singularities (edges and vertices), this paper proposes a geometrically rigorous learning framework that operates directly on meshes.
sections.details:
Manufacturing tasks such as polishing, wiping, drawing, and deburring involve continuous contact with an object's surface rather than free-space motion. Friction and surface relief play dominant roles, making it fundamentally difficult to learn these skills while ignoring surface geometry.

However, most learning from demonstration (LfD) frameworks assume flat Euclidean space, enforcing surface constraints via post-hoc normal projection, local parameterization, or force control. This fails to generalize when the underlying curvature or topology changes. Recently, geometry-aware learning on smooth Riemannian manifolds—such as rotation groups or symmetric positive-definite matrices—has advanced significantly. Yet real-world shapes from CAD or 3D scanners are polyhedral meshes rather than smooth manifolds. Mesh edges and vertices are non-differentiable singularities, causing standard smooth differential geometry tools to fail.

Existing mesh-oriented methods also rely on local approximations that avoid edges and vertices, or impose strong smoothness assumptions, limiting their robustness. Grounded in discrete differential geometry, this work derives discrete Riemannian operators that remain well-defined across mesh faces, edges, and vertices, unifying them across DMPs, GPs, and generative flow models.

sections.heading: The Rise of Geometric Learning and the Wall Posed by Discrete Meshes
sections.summary: Geometric learning on smooth manifolds is well established, but extensions to discrete meshes remain underdeveloped. Prior approaches like MeshDMP and Laplace-Beltrami operator-based spectral methods suffer from breakdown of local approximations and high computational cost, which this paper aims to resolve.
sections.details:
### Geometry-Aware Learning on Manifolds
Robot motion learning using Lie groups, Lie algebras, and Riemannian geometry has achieved notable success in learning orientations and stiffness matrices. These methods map data to a tangent space (a local flat space), learn the task, and map back to the manifold. However, they assume smooth spaces where closed-form geometric operators are available.

### Prior Methods on Discrete Meshes and Their Issues
To handle CAD and real-world environments, some studies have attempted motion planning and learning on polyhedral meshes, such as applying Riemannian Motion Policies (RMPs) or extending DMPs to meshes (MeshDMP). However, MeshDMP relies on local approximations of the exponential map (mapping tangent vectors back to the surface) restricted to infinitesimal displacements. This breaks down near vertices or where adjacent faces meet at angles exceeding 90 degrees. Furthermore, encoding the forcing term in local frames introduces drift during cyclic motions across curved surfaces.

### The Laplace-Beltrami Operator (LBO) and Its Limits
For function learning and Gaussian processes (GPs) on meshes, eigenfunction expansions of the Laplace-Beltrami operator (LBO)—the manifold counterpart of the Laplacian—have been widely used. However, this approach implicitly assumes that the mesh densely samples a smooth underlying surface, and function evaluations are restricted to mesh vertices. Evaluating values inside faces requires remeshing or interpolation, significantly driving up approximation errors and computational costs.

sections.heading: Background: Riemannian Manifolds, Meshes, and Three Learning Paradigms
sections.summary: This section reviews the three fundamental operators of Riemannian geometry (logarithmic map, exponential map, and parallel transport) and the definitions of polyhedral meshes. It also summarizes the governing equations of the three learning paradigms (DMP, GP, RFM) reformulated on meshes.
sections.details:
### Fundamental Operators on Riemannian Manifolds
The local linear approximation of a manifold $\mathbb{M}$ is its tangent space $T_p\mathbb{M}$. Moving a point on the manifold into a tangent vector is the logarithmic map ($\mathrm{Log}_p$), while projecting a tangent vector back onto the manifold is the exponential map ($\mathrm{Exp}_p$). Moving a tangent vector from one point's tangent space to another while preserving geometric properties (length and angle) is parallel transport ($P_{p\to q}$).

### Geometry of Polyhedral Meshes
This work targets 2D polyhedral surface meshes $\mathcal{M}$ embedded in 3D Euclidean space. Each face is a flat triangle, but surface normals are discontinuous across edges and vertices. Examining the total angle $\theta(p)$ subtended by faces around point $p$, interior face points and edges satisfy $\theta=2\pi$ (flat). At vertices $\nu_i$, $\theta$ equals the sum of incident face angles, categorizing vertices into spherical ($\theta<2\pi$), flat ($\theta=2\pi$), and hyperbolic ($\theta>2\pi$) points.

### Overview of the Three Learning Models
- **Geometry-aware DMP**: A dynamical system coupling a second-order spring-damper model with a learnable forcing term $f$, balancing convergence toward an attractor $g$ on the surface with desired trajectory shape.
- **Gaussian Process (GP) on Manifolds**: A Bayesian regression model taking mesh locations as inputs to predict unknown functions, where designing a positive-definite kernel is central.
- **Riemannian Flow Matching (RFM)**: A generative model where a neural network learns a time-continuous vector field that pushes a simple base distribution into the target data distribution.

sections.heading: Discrete Riemannian Operators on Meshes and Unifying Three Learning Paradigms
sections.summary: The authors mathematically define tangent cones, straightest-geodesic exponential maps, and parallel transport that remain valid at edges and vertices. These enable DMPs trained within a fixed tangent cone, GPs using geodesic distance kernels, and mesh-native RFM trained directly on geodesic paths.
sections.details:
### IV-A Design of Discrete Differential Operators
To handle singularities on meshes, the following operators are formulated:
- **Tangent Cone ($T_p\mathcal{M}$)**: Generalizes tangent spaces: a standard 2D tangent plane inside a face, two half-planes joined at an edge, or a conical space spanned by all incident triangles at a vertex.
- **Logarithmic Map**: Finds the shortest geodesic $\gamma$ from $p$ to $q$ via the continuous Dijkstra algorithm and returns the initial tangent direction vector.
- **Exponential Map (Straightest Geodesic Algorithm)**: When marching along a tangent vector, crossing edges or vertices uses the Polthier-Schmies straightest geodesic principle. By intrinsically rotating the heading such that angles on both sides are equal (bisecting the total angle as $\theta/2$), unique geodesic paths are traced through singularities (Algorithm 1).
- **Parallel Transport**: Computes a 3D rotation matrix $R$ tracking surface normals along geodesic $\gamma$, performing isometric vector transport between tangent cones.
- **Ambient-Space Projection**: Defines a projection operator from $\mathbb{R}^3$ back onto the tangent cone (Algorithm 2), ensuring compatibility with standard neural network outputs.

### IV-B Geometry-Aware DMP with a Fixed Tangent Cone
Prior MeshDMP defined forcing terms in moving local frames aligned with the instantaneous velocity, causing drift over repeated cycles. The proposed method learns forcing term $f$ in a single fixed space—the tangent cone $T_g\mathcal{M}$ of the attractor (or cycle center) $g$—and parallel-transports it ($P_{g\to p}$) to current position $p$ during execution. This stabilizes transfer of flat demonstrations onto surfaces of arbitrary curvature.

### IV-C Geodesic Distance-Based Gaussian Process (GP)
Eliminating expensive eigenfunction expansions, the method uses a squared-exponential kernel directly over mesh geodesic distances $d_g$: $k(p,q)=\sigma^2 \exp(-d_g(p,q)^2 / (2\kappa^2))$. While geodesic kernels risk losing positive definiteness beyond a lengthscale threshold $\kappa_{th}$, the authors propose a bisection search algorithm (Algorithm 3) to detect the maximum admissible $\kappa_{th}$, ensuring practical numerical stability.

### IV-D Riemannian Flow Matching (RFM) on Meshes
While previous RFM methods relied on ambient approximations or LBOs, this approach uses the exact mesh geodesic $\gamma$ between two points as the probability path flow. Integrating network vector fields with tangent cone projection and exponential maps guarantees that samples strictly remain on the discrete surface throughout integration.

sections.heading: Simulation Results: Superior Geometric Consistency and Computational Efficiency
sections.summary: Experiments were conducted on standard meshes like the Stanford Bunny. The DMP completely eliminated rotational drift in long cyclic trajectories; the GP achieved singularity-resilient regression on non-smooth surfaces; and RFM reduced training time by roughly a third (30 h to 20 h) while improving negative log-likelihood (NLL).
sections.details:
### V-A Comparison with MeshDMP (Figs. F8, F9)
A figure-eight trajectory demonstrated on a plane was transferred onto the Stanford Bunny mesh. Prior MeshDMP (red line) exhibited rotational drift around the center over time due to curvature effects. In contrast, the proposed method (green line) maintained a stable limit cycle because the forcing term is fixed at the attractor's tangent cone and parallel-transported. As shown in Fig. F9, when exponential-mapping long vectors on a torus, MeshDMP's local normal projection (red line) diverges from the true geodesic into ambient space, whereas the proposed method (yellow line) matches the true geodesic (green line) exactly.

### V-B GP Regression Accuracy Comparison (Fig. F10)
On a non-smooth mesh formed by three orthogonal cube faces sharing a corner vertex, the method was compared against an LBO eigenfunction-based Matérn kernel (Borovitskiy et al.). Because LBO-based methods assume smoothness, increasing mesh resolution amplified discretization errors around the corner singularity, causing mean absolute error (MAE) to deteriorate drastically as lengthscale $\kappa$ increased. In contrast, the proposed geodesic kernel retained very low MAE within the admissible threshold $\kappa_{th}$. Moreover, while LBO requires expensive prior decomposition, the proposed covariance evaluates linearly with respect to test points, running much faster on small-to-medium meshes up to ~5,000 faces.

### V-C Mesh Flow Matching (RFM) Evaluation (Fig. F12)
In learning high-frequency target distributions on the Stanford Bunny, the method was benchmarked against RFM using diffusion premetrics and biharmonic premetrics. The proposed method recorded the lowest negative log-likelihood (NLL) across all test cases. Furthermore, unlike baselines requiring projection steps back to the surface at every integration step, the proposed method marches natively on the mesh via the exponential map, reducing 100k-step training time from ~30 hours (1 day, 6 hours) down to ~20 hours.

sections.heading: Real-Robot Experiments: Transferring Hand-Drawn Paths and Autonomous Polishing on Reconstructed Meshes
sections.summary: Using a 7-DoF Franka Research 3 arm, two real-world tasks were validated: instantly transferring tablet-drawn handwriting onto various 3D-printed surfaces for pen drawing, and sponge-polishing an unknown bumpy workpiece reconstructed in real time via an RGB-D camera.
sections.details:
### VI-A Hand-Drawn Character Generalization and Drawing (Fig. F13)
Trajectories drawn by a user on a tablet GUI were learned on the fly and transferred to four 3D-printed surfaces (smooth curved surfaces as well as non-smooth conical surfaces with sharp edges), drawn using a pen held by a Franka Research 3.
- **Control Setup**: Force control maintained 5 N contact force along the pen axis, while in-plane motion used impedance control with 4,000 N/m stiffness. Tool orientation followed mesh face normals, smoothed across face transitions via a sliding-window filter to eliminate discontinuities.
- **Results**: Trajectories with 40,000 points were generated in under 5 seconds. The robot drew characters accurately without distortion across high-curvature peaks, valleys, and sharp, non-differentiable creases (Fig. F13, rightmost surface).

### VI-B Autonomous Surface Polishing on 3D-Reconstructed Meshes (Fig. F14)
In a realistic setup without prior CAD models, an Intel RealSense D405 RGB-D camera mounted on the end-effector reconstructed a mesh to polish off chalk marks.
- **Pipeline**: Chalk marks (yellow/orange) were extracted by color thresholding and fitted with polynomial curves. Point clouds around the marks were voxel-downsampled (5 mm spacing), and Poisson surface reconstruction generated a watertight mesh (1,344 vertices, 2,617 faces) online in 1 to 10 seconds.
- **Motion Generation and Execution**: A cyclic DMP (2-second period) trained on a plane was transferred to the reconstructed mesh, with its center moving along the polynomial path at 5 mm/s. The full 100 Hz position trajectory was generated in under 5 seconds. Hybrid force/impedance control applied constant contact force, successfully removing the chalk completely with a sponge.

sections.heading: Summary and Outlook: Real-World Contact Tasks Powered by Discrete Geometry
sections.summary: This work establishes a unified framework that treats surfaces as intrinsic geometric motion domains rather than post-hoc projection constraints. Despite open challenges in geodesic computational complexity and kernel positive definiteness, it marks an important step linking real-world perceptual meshes with geometric learning.
sections.details:
This study develops a discrete Riemannian operator system that rigorously resolves edge and vertex singularities on polyhedral meshes—the most prevalent surface representation in robotics—and successfully integrates it into DMPs, GPs, and RFM.

### Current Limitations
- **Geodesic Computational Complexity**: Exact geodesic queries via the continuous Dijkstra algorithm require $\mathcal{O}(N^2 \log N)$ preprocessing with respect to face count $N$, becoming a computational bottleneck on high-resolution meshes exceeding 10,000 faces.
- **Positive Definiteness of Geodesic Kernels**: Squared-exponential geodesic kernels can develop negative eigenvalues when lengthscale $\kappa$ exceeds an admissibility threshold $\kappa_{th}$. While the proposed bisection algorithm detects and avoids this numerically, deeper theoretical analysis connecting $\kappa_{th}$ to mesh curvature and topology is needed.

### Future Directions
Promising future avenues include extending the framework to learn and transfer contact force profiles alongside positions, as well as planning surgical robotic motions over deforming, time-varying meshes driven by patient respiration and organ motion.

takeaways: For surface contact tasks, generating and learning trajectories directly within the discrete Riemannian geometry of the surface provides far better transferability and stability than learning in flat space and projecting post-hoc.

Non-differentiable singularities like mesh edges and vertices can support unique, unbroken vector propagation (exponential mapping) by following the straightest geodesic principle (bisecting incident angles equally).
In mesh DMPs, learning the forcing term in the fixed tangent cone of the attractor and parallel-transporting it to current positions completely prevents rotational drift during cyclic motions.

For mesh GP regression, Laplace-Beltrami eigenfunction expansions often break down on non-smooth surfaces, whereas direct geodesic distance kernels enable accurate regression anywhere on the surface, including face interiors.
limitations: Building exact continuous-Dijkstra geodesic query structures scales at $\mathcal{O}(N^2 \log N)$ with face count $N$, posing computational bottlenecks on large meshes exceeding 10,000 faces.
Squared-exponential geodesic kernels lose positive definiteness beyond a lengthscale threshold $\kappa_{th}$, requiring bisection checks to ensure valid bounds.
Generated trajectories dictate only end-effector positions; tool normal orientations still rely on post-processing (sliding-window smoothing) to avoid angular jumps across face transitions.
